about.author: Zyphullen

automatic_checks.what: Structural checks run by a script on every build (src/audit.py, report in AUDIT-v0.8.md): every card has a colour and at least one source, links point at cards that exist, share links are exact, the data hash is the same in every file, counts match, and every source URL was fetched to see that it answers.
automatic_checks.not: They do not read the science. Passing them does not mean a claim is right, only that it is labelled, sourced and linked.

science_review.what: A science review means a person with the right expertise reads each claim against its sources and decides whether it is right, up to date and fairly coloured.
science_review.how_to_help: Every card has a Suggest a fix button (e-mail). Please check claims against the listed sources and say what looks wrong.

about.certainty_rule: green = established (known science, or a defined / proved result in Maths); orange = leading idea / partial progress; red = unknown / open problem. A link takes the colour of its less-certain end.

suggest_a_fix.subject: Echo Atlas fix: <Card name> (<card id>)
suggest_a_fix.note: Every card has a Suggest a fix button that opens a prefilled e-mail (section, card, card id, version, page link). Card ids: fntu/<id>, maths/<id>, history/<id>-<n>, cell/<id>, body/<id>, element/<symbol>, <section>/link/<from>><to>.

about.what_this_file_holds: A zoomable 3D tour through real NASA / ESA / Hubble / Webb / Planck / Gaia images, one stop per scale: Earth, the Sun, our sky (the Milky Way from inside), a spiral galaxy like ours (M101), Webb's First Deep Field and the cosmic microwave background. Each stop has its real size, the image credit and licence, sources and links to other sections.
about.already_in_this_file: This file already holds everything for this section: the facts (summary, details), the colours (certainty), the sources (title, url, type, year, link check) and the connections between ideas, including links to cards in other sections (rel / related / section_links, each with the other section name and id). Load another section file only when you want the full card on the other end of a link.
about.how_to_use: Every item has id, title, certainty, summary, details and sources (title, url, type). Full source details (year, link check) are in sources_used. A link's reason_sources are the sources on its two cards. Fact-check against the sources; flag anything that looks wrong or out of date.

universe.note: A zoomable 3D tour through real NASA / ESA images, one stop per scale. Pictures are only resized, cropped or wrapped onto a ball (all-sky maps); nothing is painted in. Sizes are on each stop, not drawn to scale with each other.

stops.title: Earth
stops.subtitle: our planet, about 12,742 km across
stops.shown_as: photo map wrapped on a ball
summary: Earth is a rocky planet with a mean radius of 6,371 km. The globe is wrapped with NASA's Blue Marble map.
details: What the picture is: A cloud-free mosaic of many satellite photos (NASA Blue Marble), not one snapshot. Real colours, real land and sea.
Size: Mean radius 6,371 km, so about 12,742 km across (NASA fact sheet).

image.credit: NASA Earth Observatory / Blue Marble · public domain

sources.title: NASA NSSDCA: Earth fact sheet
NASA Visible Earth: Blue Marble collection
Image: Whole world, land and oceans (NASA Earth Observatory / Blue Marble, public domain)

stops.title: The Sun
stops.subtitle: our star, 109 Earths across
summary: The Sun has a mean radius of 695,700 km, about 109 times Earth's. Earth orbits it at a mean distance of 149.6 million km.
details: What the picture is: A real photo by NASA's Solar Dynamics Observatory taken in extreme ultraviolet light, which our eyes cannot see, so the colours are false colours.
Size: Mean radius 695,700 km; 109.2 × Earth (NASA fact sheet). Light from the Sun takes about 8 minutes to reach us.

sources.title: NASA NSSDCA: Sun fact sheet (radius, Sun/Earth ratio, mean distance)
NASA Solar Dynamics Observatory (SDO)
Image: the Sun by SDO's Atmospheric Imaging Assembly, 19 Aug 2010 (NASA/SDO, public domain)

stops.title: Our sky: the Milky Way from inside
stops.subtitle: Gaia's map of 1.7 billion stars
stops.shown_as: all-sky map on a ball around you
summary: We live inside the Milky Way, about 27,000 light-years from its centre, so we see it as a bright band across the sky. ESA's Gaia mapped about 1.7 billion of its stars.
details: What the picture is: Gaia's all-sky map (Data Release 2), built from star measurements, wrapped on a ball around you. Look around: the bright band is the disc of our galaxy, and the two smudges lower right are the Large and Small Magellanic Clouds.
Be careful: A sky map shows directions, not distances: stars on it are at very different distances.
Where we are: The Galactic Centre is 8.178 kiloparsecs away (about 26,700 light-years), measured by the GRAVITY Collaboration in 2019.

sources.title: ESA: Gaia's sky in colour (Gaia DR2 all-sky map)
Gaia Collaboration 2018: Gaia Data Release 2, summary of the contents (A&A 616, A1)
GRAVITY Collaboration 2019: distance to the Galactic Centre, 8.178 kpc (A&A 625, L10)
Image: Gaia's all-sky view, ESA/Gaia/DPAC (CC BY 4.0)

stops.title: A spiral galaxy like ours (M101)
stops.subtitle: the Pinwheel Galaxy, 25 million light-years away
summary: No camera has ever left the Milky Way, so nobody has a photo of our galaxy from outside. M101, the Pinwheel Galaxy, is a real spiral galaxy seen face-on by Hubble.
details: What the picture is: Hubble's largest galaxy portrait: 51 exposures plus ground-based images (ESA/Hubble, 2006). The photo is flat; real galaxy discs are thin but not flat paper.
Size and distance: About 170,000 light-years across, nearly twice the Milky Way, and about 25 million light-years away (ESA/Hubble).
Honest note: Our galaxy is a barred spiral; M101 is used here only as a real example of what a spiral galaxy looks like.

image.credit: European Space Agency & NASA · CC BY 4.0

sources.title: ESA/Hubble heic0602: largest ever Hubble galaxy portrait, the Pinwheel Galaxy (M101)
Image: M101, European Space Agency & NASA (CC BY 4.0)

stops.title: Galaxies everywhere: Webb's First Deep Field
stops.subtitle: thousands of galaxies in a grain-of-sand patch of sky
stops.shown_as: flat photo of a patch of sky
summary: Point a big telescope at a tiny dark patch of sky and it fills with galaxies. This patch is about the size of a grain of sand held at arm's length.
details: What the picture is: NASA's Webb telescope, infrared camera NIRCam, 12.5 hours. Infrared light is shown as visible colours.
What you see: The galaxy cluster SMACS 0723 as it was 4.6 billion years ago. Its gravity bends light from galaxies far behind it into arcs (gravitational lensing).
Honest note: This is a flat photo. The galaxies in it are at many different distances; we do not show them in 3D.

image.credit: NASA, ESA, CSA, STScI · public domain

sources.title: NASA / STScI: Webb's First Deep Field (NIRCam image of SMACS 0723)
Image: Webb's First Deep Field, NASA, ESA, CSA, STScI (public domain)

stops.title: The oldest light: the cosmic microwave background
stops.subtitle: ESA Planck's map of the whole sky
stops.shown_as: all-sky map on a ball around us
stops.size: the edge of what we can see
summary: The farthest thing we can see is light released about 380,000 years after the Big Bang. ESA's Planck mapped it across the whole sky.
details: What the picture is: Planck's all-sky map of tiny temperature differences in the cosmic microwave background, wrapped on a ball with us at the centre. Microwaves are invisible, so the colours are false colours.
How far: Because space has expanded, the matter that sent this light is now about 46 billion light-years away: roughly the radius of the observable universe.
Honest note: It is a sphere around us because we see out in every direction; it is not a wall at the edge of the universe.

image.credit: ESA and the Planck Collaboration · CC BY 4.0
